name: Igari blush

lead: Igari blush places colour under the eyes and across both cheeks and over the nose bridge, resembling a flush after a drink, hence the nicknames drunk blush and hangover makeup. It makes the face look warm, fresh and youthful with otherwise minimal makeup.
It is named for Japanese makeup artist Shinobu Igari and spread widely on TikTok. It is a beauty trend rather than a researched technique.

paras: Guides describe light base and concealer, natural brows, no contouring, then cream or powder blush in pink, peach or rose built up gradually across the cheeks and nose, often with a matching lip colour and optional faux freckles.
Low-risk cosmetic styling; as with any makeup, irritation is possible from individual products. Heavy colour can read differently across skin tones and lighting.

chain: Blush placed under eyes and across the nose
angle.text: The blush placement adds colour across the midface, giving a warm, healthy-looking flush. Proponents say it suits many skin tones and pairs with minimal makeup.

lead: Igari blush, also called drunk blush or hangover makeup, is a style in which blush extends beyond the apples of the cheeks to cross the bridge of the nose, mimicking a natural flush [1]. The effect is a soft, youthful, warm face with little other makeup.

The look is named after makeup artist Igari Shinobu and is reported to have begun in Japan in 2018, following eras of large-eye and heavily contoured makeup [1]. It spread mainly through TikTok tutorials and duets [1].
infobox: Cream or powder blush in pink, peach, rose [1]

paras: Guides describe a minimalist base, light brows and mascara, no contouring, and cream or powder blush applied from below the eyes across the nose, built gradually [1]. Cream blush is said to blend more easily and look more natural, while powder over it extends wear [1]. Freckles, real or drawn, and a matching lip colour are optional [1].

Beauty publications attribute the style to Igari Shinobu and to a shift away from the big-eye and contoured looks of the mid-2000s and early 2010s [1]. Retail guides call it a Japanese trend that tied into kawaii aesthetics and skin-focused beauty [1].

timeline.event: Igari makeup reported to emerge in Japan, named for Shinobu Igari [1].
